cards.t: The chest radiograph as the first study
q: why is a chest x-ray ordered first
what is the most common imaging study
when do you get a chest radiograph
cards.x:
The chest radiograph is the most common radiologic study, and it is almost always the first study for a pulmonary or cardiac complaint. Radiographs make up 75% of all radiology images ordered in the United States, and the two complaints most tied to a chest film are pain and shortness of breath.

The film comes first, and what it shows decides whether anything more, such as computed tomography, is needed. The one exception is a suspected pulmonary embolism, where a computed tomography angiogram comes first.

cards.t: Posteroanterior vs anteroposterior chest films
q: what is the difference between a PA and an AP chest x-ray
why does the heart look bigger on an AP film
which chest film is taken standing
cards.x:
These are the two frontal chest views, named for the direction the beam travels. A posteroanterior (PA) film is taken with the patient standing and ambulatory, chest against the plate, so the beam enters from the back. An anteroposterior (AP) film is taken with the patient supine, often in bed as a portable film, so the beam enters from the front.

The practical difference is the heart: the anteroposterior view magnifies it. So a heart that looks big on an anteroposterior film is not, by itself, an enlarged heart. Know which view you are looking at before you judge heart size.

cards.t: The aortic knob
q: what is the aortic knob
where is the aortic knob on a chest x-ray
what is the bulge at the top left of the heart shadow
cards.x:
The aortic knob is the aortic arch as it shows on a frontal chest film: the rounded bulge at the top of the left mediastinal border. It is one of the landmarks to find on every film.

Stacked below it along the left border are the pulmonary artery (the pulmonary trunk) and then the left hilum, with the left ventricle forming the lower left heart border down to the diaphragm. Remember that films are viewed as if you are facing the patient, so the patient's left side, and the knob, sit on your right.

cards.t: The costophrenic angles
q: what is the costophrenic angle
what does a blunted costophrenic angle mean
what should the costophrenic angles look like
cards.x:
The costophrenic angles are the sharp V shapes where each hemidiaphragm meets the side wall of the chest on a frontal film. On a normal film they are nice and sharp.

When fluid collects in the pleural space the V is filled in and lost: that blunting is the classic sign of a pleural effusion. Don't confuse it with the cardiophrenic angle, which is the inner corner where the heart border meets the diaphragm.

cards.t: Normal structures on the frontal chest film
q: what structures should I find on a normal chest x-ray
what is the dark bubble under the left diaphragm
which heart chamber forms the right border on x-ray
cards.x:
A normal frontal film has a predictable map. The trachea is a dark air column in the midline that divides at the carina into the main bronchi. On the left border sit the aortic knob, the pulmonary artery and the left hilum; the left ventricle forms the lower left heart border, and the right atrium forms the right heart border. The pulmonary markings fan out from the hila, and the superior and inferior vena cava lie on the right.

At the bottom are the two hemidiaphragm domes: the liver under the right one and the gastric bubble (gas in the stomach) under the left. The images are always viewed as if you are facing the patient, so the patient's left is on your right.

cards.t: The systematic read of a chest film
k: how to read a chest x-ray
q: how do you read a chest x-ray step by step
what should I look at on a chest film
how should ribs be checked on a chest x-ray
cards.x:
Read every film in the same order so nothing gets skipped:

- Lung fields: dark (radiolucent) because they are full of air; trace each lung's margin, then sweep across it, comparing left with right.
- The retrosternal and retrocardiac spaces, best seen on the lateral film.
- Heart size: no more than half the posteroanterior width of the chest.
- Vascular markings: only the pulmonary arteries and veins should be visible.
- Ribs one at a time, both sides, before moving down; spinous processes in the midline; the trachea and main bronchi smooth-edged, dark inside, and in the midline.

cards.t: Heart size and the one-third, two-thirds rule
q: how big should the heart be on a chest x-ray
what is the one third two thirds rule
how do you judge heart size on a PA film
cards.x:
On a posteroanterior film the heart should be no more than half the width of the chest. The one-third, two-thirds rule describes where it sits: about one third of the heart lies to the right of the midline and two thirds to the left.

Two cautions keep you from overcalling it. The rule is judged on a posteroanterior film; a supine anteroposterior film magnifies the heart. And in pulmonary edema a larger cardiothoracic ratio is one of the signs, so a heart wider than half the chest on a proper posteroanterior film is a real finding.

cards.t: The hila on a chest film
q: why is the left hilum higher
what makes up the hilum on a chest x-ray
where should the hila be on a chest film
cards.x:
The hilum is the junction point where the pulmonary vessels and the bronchus enter each lung. On a frontal film each hilum sits halfway down, bisecting the chest, with about as much lung above it as below.

It is mostly the pulmonary arteries and veins, with some fat, lymph nodes and bronchial walls. The two should be concave in shape and similar in size and density, and the left hilum is normally slightly higher than the right, so a higher left hilum is not a finding. On the checklist, the hila are checked for masses and lymphadenopathy.

cards.t: The lateral chest film
q: what does a lateral chest x-ray show
where is the retrocardiac space
what should the spine look like on a lateral chest film
cards.x:
The lateral film is the side view of the chest. It shows two spaces the frontal film hides: the retrosternal space, behind the sternum and in front of the heart, and the retrocardiac space, behind the heart.

You can also follow the trachea, the aortic arch and the pulmonary artery, with the right ventricle at the front of the heart and the left ventricle at the back. The normal thoracic spine on this view has a posterior arch, with the disc spaces present and symmetric.

cards.t: When to order a skull or soft-tissue neck film
q: when do you order a soft tissue neck x-ray
what is stridor
how do you read a neck x-ray
cards.x:
A facial, skull or soft-tissue neck radiograph is indicated for a muffled voice, stridor (wheezing heard through the patient's mouth without a stethoscope), a suspected sinus infection, and anterior neck pain.

Read it from top to bottom, sweeping left to right and comparing as you go down. The airways should be dark because they hold air, the sinuses should be air-filled, the bones should be continuous, the cervical spine should have a slight forward curve (normal lordosis), and both sides should be symmetric.

cards.t: The Water's view of the sinuses
q: what is the Water's view
which sinuses does the Water's view show
do you need an x-ray for sinusitis
cards.x:
The Water's view is a frontal skull film angled 45 degrees to the orbitomeatal line, used for the maxillary and frontal sinuses. Air-filled sinuses show dark on it.

For a suspected sinus infection the film is not really needed, but it can help confirm the infection and possibly reduce antibiotic use. So it is an optional confirmation step, not a requirement before treatment.

cards.t: The lateral soft-tissue neck film
q: what does a normal lateral neck x-ray show
why is there no air in the esophagus on a neck x-ray
where is the esophagus on a lateral neck film
cards.x:
The lateral soft-tissue neck film shows the airway and the soft tissues around it from the side. From top to bottom you can find the nasopharyngeal space, the retropharyngeal space, the epiglottis and vallecula, the hyoid bone, the vocal cords, the trachea, and the seventh cervical vertebra (C7).

The trachea is the dark, open column, dark because it is full of air. The esophagus sits behind it in the retrotracheal space and normally shows no air at all: it is collapsed, which is what it should be when the person is not eating. The cervical spine has a slight forward curve, and the vertebral body below C7 is partly hidden because the first rib overlaps it.

cards.t: Computed tomography planes
q: what are the planes on a CT scan
how do I tell a sagittal from a coronal CT
what is a lung window
cards.x:
A computed tomography (CT) image is a slice, not a shadow of everything stacked together like a radiograph. Know the three planes on sight:

- Transverse (axial): a cross-section, like a slice of bread, showing both lungs, the mediastinum and the vertebra.
- Frontal (coronal): both lungs side by side, from apex to base, as if facing the patient.
- Sagittal: one side in profile, front to back, with the spine down one edge.

The lung window is a display setting that shows the lung tissue in high detail; in it the trachea and bronchi are dark circles because they are full of air.

cards.t: Finding your way on a computed tomography angiogram
q: how do you orient yourself on a CT angiogram
where is the descending aorta on CT
which ventricle is closest to the sternum
cards.x:
A pulmonary vasculogram is almost always a computed tomography (CT) angiogram, a scan with contrast that makes the vessels bright. They are hard to read and are left to the radiologist, but a few pearls keep you oriented:

- Lost? Find the descending aorta, a bright round vessel that is always on the left side of the patient's vertebral column.
- In the transverse view the patient's left is always on your right.
- The heart sits more to the patient's left; the right ventricle is closest to the sternum, and the left ventricle always has the thickest wall.
- When looking for an embolism or clot, the pulmonary arteries matter most.

cards.t: The sternal angle and the nipple line
q: which rib is at the sternal angle
what intercostal space is the nipple line
how do you find the second rib
cards.x:
These are the two chest landmarks you can feel. The sternal angle (the manubriosternal joint, the ridge where the top piece of the breastbone meets the body) lines up with the second rib. That is how you find the second rib for procedures and where you start to count the ribs down. The nipple line corresponds to the fifth intercostal space.

The fifth rib also divides the lobes: below the base of the fifth rib are the inferior lobes, and above it are the superior lobes.

cards.t: Neck landmarks and the triangles of the neck
q: what is in the posterior triangle of the neck
what lies deep to the jugular notch
at what vertebral level is the larynx
cards.x:
A few surface points tell you what lies underneath. Deep to the jugular notch is the trachea. The larynx sits from the third to the sixth cervical vertebra, and about 1 centimeter below the laryngeal prominence is the cricothyroid ligament.

The sternocleidomastoid divides the neck into an anterior and a posterior triangle. The posterior triangle contains the subclavian vein and the lung apices (the tops of the lungs). The carotid triangle, part of the anterior triangle, contains the bifurcation of the common carotid artery.

cards.t: Checking the bones on chest films
q: how do you check the ribs on a chest x-ray
what is the best imaging for rib fractures
what should the spine look like on a chest film
cards.x:
The bones are checked for lesions or fractures, always comparing the two sides for symmetry. Go through the ribs one at a time, both sides, before moving down to the next; the spinous processes should sit in the midline. On a lateral chest film the thoracic spine has a gentle posterior arch with even disc spaces; on a lateral neck film the cervical spine has a slight forward curve, and the first rib partly hides the vertebra below the seventh cervical vertebra (C7).

If a radiograph is inconclusive for a rib or spinal fracture, computed tomography is the next study, because it is the best imaging modality for bone.

cards.t: Overexposed vs underexposed chest films
q: how can you tell if a chest x-ray is overexposed
what does an underexposed film look like
why can I see the spine through the heart
cards.x:
Exposure changes how dark the whole picture is. A well-exposed film shows the vessels out to at least the outer third of the lung, the edges along the spine, and the left hemidiaphragm behind the heart.

- Overexposed: too dark. The thoracic spine, the mediastinum and the areas behind the heart show through, and so do nasogastric and endotracheal tubes, which is why that exposure helps you trace a tube.
- Underexposed: too white. The vessels look small and you cannot see the spine or the mediastinal anatomy.

Check exposure before calling the lungs abnormal.

cards.t: Inspiration and rotation on a chest film
q: how many ribs should you see on a chest x-ray
how do you tell if a chest film is rotated
why not use the trachea to check rotation
cards.x:
Two more technique checks before you call anything abnormal. Inspiration: a deep breath pulls the diaphragm down so you see as much lung as possible; on a standing film the domes should reach the tenth posterior rib (eighth to tenth when seated or lying). Only a few ribs above the diaphragm means poor effort, which hides lung.

Rotation: measure the distance from the center spinous processes to the borders of each clavicle; they should be equal. Never use the tracheal shadow, because the trachea is a tube and looks the same when the patient is turned.

cards.t: The radiographic anatomy checklist
k: what to look for on chest x-ray
q: what abnormalities do you look for on a chest x-ray
what is the pleura checked for
what are the hila checked for on a chest film
cards.x:
Each structure on the film has its own abnormal finding to look for:

- Trachea: midline or deviated; a deviated trachea is abnormal. Also caliber and any mass.
- Lungs: abnormal shadowing or lucency. Pulmonary vessels: artery or vein enlargement.
- Hila: masses or lymphadenopathy. Mediastinum: width or a mass. Heart: width against the chest and its shape.
- Pleura: effusion, thickening, calcification. Bones: lesions or fractures, always checking symmetry.
- Soft tissues: don't miss a mastectomy.

cards.t: Indications for a chest radiograph
q: when should I order a chest x-ray
how long a cough needs a chest x-ray
when is CT first instead of an x-ray
cards.x:
A chest radiograph is indicated for chest pain, shortness of breath, dyspnea on exertion, any cough lasting more than 6 weeks with no explanation, unexplained weight loss in any chronic smoker, hemoptysis (coughing up blood), abnormal lung sounds on listening, and checking support hardware such as lines, tubes or a pacemaker. There are others.

These may lead on to computed tomography, but the radiograph comes first and its findings decide. Computed tomography comes first only for a suspected pulmonary embolism, as a computed tomography angiogram.

cards.t: Radiation safety, pregnancy and lead shielding
q: are there contraindications to a chest x-ray
do you need a pregnancy test before an x-ray
can a pregnant patient get a CT
cards.x:
Radiographs have no true contraindications, and imaging in general has few. The safeguards are about dose and sensitive tissue. The recommended lifetime limit for diagnostic radiation is 100 millisieverts, about 10,000 chest radiographs or 25 chest computed tomography scans.

Always order a beta human chorionic gonadotropin (pregnancy) urine or blood test for every female of childbearing age. Pregnancy is a caution, not an absolute contraindication: in an emergency such as a pulmonary embolism, imaging is done, even with contrast. Lead-shield everything not being filmed, especially the thyroid, ovaries, testes, breasts and a fetus.

cards.t: Pulmonary ultrasound
q: when is lung ultrasound used
what are the contraindications to lung ultrasound
what does lung ultrasound look like
cards.x:
Pulmonary ultrasound is used almost exclusively in trauma, to look quickly for a collapsed lung (pneumothorax) or fluid. It is done at the bedside in the emergency department and trauma bay as part of the extended focused assessment with sonography for trauma, and it can guide procedures. It has no contraindications.

On the image, each rib casts a dark shadow beneath it. Between the ribs is the bright pleural line, with the lung tissue below it, and that pleural line is where the study looks.

cards.t: High and low attenuation on computed tomography
q: what does high attenuation mean on CT
is blood bright or dark on CT
why is contrast bright on CT
cards.x:
Attenuation is how much a tissue blocks the beam. High attenuation shows bright and low attenuation shows dark, the computed tomography version of radiopaque and radiolucent on a film.

- High (bright): bone, which is very high; fresh blood from a hemorrhage; and contrast material, which is exactly why contrast is used, to show areas a plain scan may miss.
- Normal: heart and muscle.
- Low (dark): air and gas, fluid, and blood that has already clotted (it clots quickly in the lungs).

cards.t: When to order chest computed tomography
q: when should I get a chest CT
what is the most common reason for chest CT
when do you get a CT of the neck
cards.x:
The most common reason for chest computed tomography (CT) is an inconclusive radiograph in a patient whose lung problem continues. Other indications are a suspected pulmonary embolism, trauma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and interstitial lung disease, bone (it is the best study to rule out rib and spine fractures), and cancer screening.

Computed tomography of the head and neck is done for a possible upper airway obstruction, such as a retropharyngeal abscess or a foreign body the radiograph missed.

cards.t: Contrast: when it is used and when to be careful
q: when do you use contrast for a CT
is shellfish allergy a contraindication to contrast
why does creatinine matter before contrast
cards.x:
Contrast lights up the vessels, so it is used when you need to see them: suspected vascular problems (pulmonary embolism, dissection, aneurysm), a focal lesion such as a tumor or abscess, the -itis conditions (for vasculitis magnetic resonance is superior), and metastases, because it shows involved lymph nodes, of which the neck has a great many.

Cautions before contrast: anaphylaxis to medicines; anaphylaxis to shellfish when iodine allergy has not been tested; anaphylaxis or angioedema to iodine; a high creatinine or blood urea nitrogen, because contrast is cleared by the kidneys and is nephrotoxic; and suspected thyroid dysfunction.

cards.t: Positron emission and single-photon emission tomography
q: what is a PET scan used for
what is the difference between PET and SPECT
why is PET combined with CT
cards.x:
These are nuclear scans that use a radioactive tracer. Positron emission tomography (PET) has higher resolution and higher sensitivity than single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT), and it costs more. Both are used fairly often but usually after the chest radiograph, not instead of it.

Positron emission tomography is mostly used to find cancer metastases; because the lungs are a common site of spread, it matters in many cancers, not just lung cancer. It is now done mostly as a combined scan with computed tomography, which gives a much clearer image.

cards.t: The ventilation/perfusion scan
q: what is a VQ scan
when do you use a VQ scan instead of CT angiogram
how is a ventilation perfusion scan done
cards.x:
The ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) scan looks for a pulmonary embolism by comparing where air goes with where blood goes. For the ventilation half the patient inhales a radioactive tracer, technetium-99m, and is imaged; for the perfusion half technetium-99m macroaggregated albumin is injected into a vein and the patient is imaged again. A clot shows as lung that is ventilated but not perfused.

It is inferior to the computed tomography angiogram and is used when the angiogram cannot be done, mainly because of a contrast allergy. The result is reported as a low, medium or high probability of pulmonary embolism, and the radiologist reads it.

cards.t: Magnetic resonance imaging of the chest
q: when is MRI used for the lungs
what are the contraindications to MRI
why is CT preferred over MRI for the lungs
cards.x:
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is the best study for soft tissue, but the lungs' unique anatomy makes computed tomography usually the first choice, even when ruling out cancer. So there are not many primary lung indications. Magnetic resonance is used for a mass that was inconclusive on computed tomography, for patients who cannot have computed tomography, as a second choice for vessel disease, and it is superior to the computed tomography angiogram for an intramural hematoma (blood collected between the layers of the artery wall).

Precautions: metal implants that are not titanium, allergy to gadolinium contrast (rare), and claustrophobia. On the two main weightings, T1 (shorter intervals between pulses) and T2 (longer intervals), inflammation is dark on T1 and bright on T2, and air is always very dark.

cards.t: Pneumonia on imaging
q: what does pneumonia look like on a chest x-ray
what is consolidation
can you tell bacterial from viral pneumonia on x-ray
cards.x:
Pneumonia shows as consolidation (also called an infiltrate): white, filled-in lung where the air-filled lung should be dark. On computed tomography it is the same idea, a dense, filled-in area within the affected lobe.

Bacterial, viral and coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pneumonia can each look different on a film, but sorting them by picture is not the goal. The patient's history and how sick they look tell those apart; the film tells you the lung is filled in.

cards.t: Pleural effusion on imaging
q: what does a pleural effusion look like on x-ray
what are blunted costophrenic angles
how do you tell effusion from consolidation
cards.x:
A pleural effusion is fluid collecting in the pleural space, between the layers of the pleura around the lung. On a chest film the hallmark is blunted costophrenic angles: the normally sharp V at each base fills in and is lost. On computed tomography it is a gray collection in the pleural space that compresses the lung.

On a film alone an effusion can be hard to tell from consolidation, so the history matters: shortness of breath, an older patient, or heart failure all raise the suspicion of fluid.

cards.t: Pulmonary edema and Kerley B lines
q: what does pulmonary edema look like on x-ray
what are Kerley B lines
what is cephalization
cards.x:
Pulmonary edema is fluid in the lungs, and a chest film shows four signs together:

- Cephalization of vessels: the vessels in the upper lungs become prominent.
- Kerley B lines: short, thin, horizontal lines at the outer edges of the lower lungs, caused by thickening of the interlobular septa (the thin walls between the lung's tiny lobules).
- A pleural effusion.
- An increased cardiothoracic ratio, a heart wider against the chest than it should be.

Kerley B lines can show on computed tomography too. Quick way to tell them from an effusion: the lines sit in the lung's edge, while an effusion fills in the costophrenic angle.

cards.t: Pneumothorax on imaging
q: what does a pneumothorax look like on x-ray
how do you see a collapsed lung on CT
what is the black area next to the lung
cards.x:
A pneumothorax is air in the pleural space, outside the lung. On a chest film that air is jet black, with no lung markings in it, and the compressed lung sits beside it. On computed tomography it is the same picture in cross-section: black air filling the pleural space, with the compressed lung beside it.

In trauma, a bedside ultrasound is the quick way to look for it.

cards.t: Interstitial lung disease on imaging
q: what does interstitial lung disease look like on x-ray
what is honeycombing
what are ground glass opacities
cards.x:
Interstitial lung disease (ILD) affects the lung tissue between the air sacs, the interstitium, rather than the air sacs themselves. On a chest film it shows as diffuse, abnormal patterns through the lungs; the first job is simply to recognize that it doesn't look right. On computed tomography the report uses these terms:

- Reticular opacities: a net-like lattice. Nodular pattern: tiny dots or bumps.
- Honeycombing: ring-like or cystic spaces, usually 3 to 10 millimeters.
- Volume loss: shrunken lung fields or raised diaphragms.
- Traction bronchiectasis: airways pulled open by surrounding scarring.
- Ground-glass opacities: hazy, pale areas of increased density. Kerley B lines can appear too.

cards.t: The arterial blood gas and what an order includes
q: what is an arterial blood gas
what does an arterial blood gas order include
what values come back on a blood gas
cards.x:
An arterial blood gas is a blood sample taken from an artery that gives an assessment of normal body function and balance (homeostasis). It is often used in combination with vital signs, the physical examination, blood drawn from a vein (the complete blood count, the comprehensive metabolic panel and others), fluid intake, urine output and more.

An order usually includes the pH; the pressures of carbon dioxide and oxygen; the oxygen saturation; carbon dioxide content and oxygen content; the base excess or deficit; bicarbonate; hemoglobin and hematocrit; carboxyhemoglobin; and the electrolytes sodium, potassium, calcium and chloride. Labs differ, so always verify what an order contains with the lab you are using.

cards.t: Partial pressure of carbon dioxide (what it measures)
q: what does the carbon dioxide pressure on a blood gas mean
what does pCO2 tell you
why is carbon dioxide used to judge ventilation
cards.x:
The partial pressure of carbon dioxide is the pressure exerted by carbon dioxide dissolved in the blood. Think of it as the lungs' report card for getting carbon dioxide out: it shows how well gas exchange is working in the air sacs (the alveoli).

It indicates the rate and depth of breathing, so it assesses alveolar ventilation, meaning how well air is being moved through the air sacs. It is used to detect respiratory abnormalities and, together with the pH, to determine whether the blood is too acidic or too alkaline.

cards.t: Partial pressure of oxygen (dissolved oxygen)
q: what does the oxygen pressure on a blood gas measure
does the oxygen pressure include oxygen on hemoglobin
what is the partial pressure of oxygen used for
cards.x:
The partial pressure of oxygen is the pressure exerted by oxygen dissolved in blood plasma. It only counts the dissolved oxygen: less than 2% of the oxygen your blood carries is dissolved in plasma, and 98% is bound to hemoglobin. So it is a narrow window, not the total oxygen on board.

What it does tell you is how much oxygen is passing from the air sacs into the blood. That makes it the value for judging the lungs' ability to oxygenate blood, and for checking whether oxygen therapy is working. Remember it depends directly on the fraction of inspired oxygen, so you always need to know what the patient was breathing.

cards.t: Oxygen saturation vs oxygen content vs oxygen capacity
q: what is the difference between oxygen saturation and oxygen content
what is oxygen capacity
does oxygen saturation tell you how much oxygen is in the blood
cards.x:
These three are easy to blur, so line them up as a fraction. Oxygen capacity is the maximum amount of oxygen that can combine with hemoglobin. Oxygen content is the actual amount of oxygen in the blood, normally 15 to 22 mL per dL in arterial blood and 11 to 16 in venous blood. Oxygen saturation is the ratio of the oxygen actually on hemoglobin to that maximum, so capacity is the denominator.

The catch: saturation shows the relationship between oxygen and hemoglobin, not the oxygen content. It is also measured by pulse oximetry. Whenever you read it, know the patient's fraction of inspired oxygen, meaning room air or supplemental oxygen.

cards.t: Carboxyhemoglobin and carbon monoxide poisoning
q: what is carboxyhemoglobin
why does carbon monoxide bind hemoglobin
what is a normal carboxyhemoglobin level
cards.x:
Carboxyhemoglobin is hemoglobin that has picked up carbon monoxide instead of oxygen. Hemoglobin grabs carbon monoxide 240 times more tightly than it grabs oxygen, so carbon monoxide competes very strongly with oxygen for hemoglobin.

The result shows how much carbon monoxide poisoning is present. Normal is less than 2% of total hemoglobin. Smokers run higher: about 4% to 5% in light smokers and 6% to 8% in heavy smokers.

cards.t: Carbon dioxide as the driver of breathing
q: what controls the rate of breathing
why would carbon dioxide rise without faster breathing
what impairs the respiratory center
cards.x:
Carbon dioxide in the blood and cerebrospinal fluid is the major chemical factor regulating ventilation. As carbon dioxide rises, ventilation increases, so breathing speeds up to blow it off. Extreme increases in the fraction of inspired carbon dioxide (more than 5%) can instead cause respiratory depression.

That gives you a useful pattern. If carbon dioxide keeps climbing but the breathing rate does not rise to meet it, suspect the respiratory center itself. Head trauma, anesthesia, and drugs such as narcotics and barbiturates can impair that center, so the brain stops responding to the rising carbon dioxide.

cards.t: The fraction of inspired oxygen and the oxygen pressure
q: how does supplemental oxygen change the blood gas
why note room air on a blood gas sample
what is the fraction of inspired oxygen
cards.x:
The fraction of inspired oxygen is the amount of oxygen in the air being taken into the lungs. It directly affects the oxygen pressure on a blood gas. Giving more oxygen (supplemental oxygen) is a cause of a higher oxygen pressure, and an insufficient fraction of inspired oxygen is a cause of a low one.

This is why a blood gas result cannot be read in a vacuum. An oxygen pressure that looks good may only reflect oxygen being given, and one that looks poor may reflect too little oxygen in the air breathed. Every sample is sent labeled with room air or a description of the supplemental oxygen.

cards.t: Volatile vs nonvolatile acids (where hydrogen ions come from)
q: what is the difference between volatile and nonvolatile acids
where do hydrogen ions in blood come from
which acids cause metabolic acidosis
cards.x:
pH is the negative logarithm of the hydrogen ion concentration in blood, so the question is where the hydrogen ions come from. There are two sources.

- Volatile acids, for example carbonic acid. They can vary between liquid and gas.
- Nonvolatile acids, for example dietary acids, lactic acid and ketoacids.

The classic nonvolatile acids to remember are ketoacids (as in diabetic ketoacidosis) and lactic acid.

cards.t: The oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve
q: what does the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve show
why does hemoglobin release oxygen in the tissues
where do blood leaving the lungs and returning blood sit on the curve
cards.x:
The curve shows how tightly hemoglobin holds oxygen at different oxygen pressures. Where the pressure is high, as in the pulmonary capillaries of the lungs, oxygen binds with hemoglobin. Where it is low, as in the tissue capillaries, oxygen is released from hemoglobin.

You can see this on the curve. Oxygenated blood leaving the lungs sits high on the flat upper part, at high oxygen pressure where oxygen binds. Reduced blood returning from the tissues sits on the steep lower part, at low oxygen pressure where oxygen is released. The same hemoglobin therefore loads up in the lungs and unloads where the body needs it.

cards.t: Left shift vs right shift of the oxygen-hemoglobin curve
q: what causes a right shift of the oxygen dissociation curve
what does a left shift mean
how does pH change how hemoglobin holds oxygen
cards.x:
A shift changes how willing hemoglobin is to hold oxygen. Quick memory line: left shift, hemoglobin holds on to oxygen; right shift, it lets go.

- Left shift: tied to a high pH (alkalosis). Oxygen bonds more tightly to hemoglobin.
- Right shift: tied to a low pH (acidosis). Oxygen is released more easily from hemoglobin.

The curve shifts to the right with increased hydrogen ions, increased carbon dioxide, increased temperature and increased 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate. On the curves for pH 7.6, 7.4 and 7.2, the alkaline 7.6 curve sits to the left and the acidic 7.2 curve sits to the right.

cards.t: Base excess or deficit (whole blood buffer base)
q: what is base excess
what does a negative base excess mean
why is base excess useful on a blood gas
cards.x:
Base excess, also called the whole blood buffer base, is the sum of the concentration of buffer anions in whole blood. Bicarbonate makes up half of those buffers; the other half is other anions such as plasma proteins and phosphates. It is critically important for telling respiratory changes apart from nonrespiratory changes in acid-base balance.

- Positive number: a base excess, meaning a nonvolatile acid deficit or a true base excess.
- Negative number: a base deficit, meaning a metabolic disturbance or nonvolatile acid excess, for example lactic acidosis or ketoacidosis, or a true base deficit.

cards.t: Why use arterial blood instead of venous blood
q: why do we draw arterial blood for a blood gas
what are the limits of venous blood
what does arterial blood tell you that venous does not
cards.x:
Arterial blood provides a better mixture of blood. Venous blood is best for information that is more localized to the draw site, and it can be affected by temperature, perfusion, movement and local infection.

Arterial blood indicates how well the lungs are oxygenating blood and whether the heart and circulation are failing.

One limit: arterial blood does not indicate the degree of any abnormality. You still need a physical assessment of the patient. The rule is to treat the patient and not the labs.

cards.t: Venous blood gas values vs arterial values
q: what are normal venous blood gas values
is a carbon dioxide of 50 normal
why are venous values different from arterial
cards.x:
Venous blood has its own normal ranges, and you read each value against the range for its own sample.

- Carbon dioxide pressure: arterial 35 to 45 mm Hg; venous 41 to 57 mm Hg (higher).
- Oxygen pressure: venous 30 to 40 mm Hg, far lower than arterial.
- pH: arterial 7.35 to 7.45; venous 7.31 to 7.41 (lower).
- Oxygen content: arterial 15 to 22 vol%; venous 11 to 16 vol% (lower).

So a venous carbon dioxide of 50 mm Hg is normal for venous blood, even though it would be high for an arterial sample.

cards.t: The radial artery and the Allen test
q: what is the Allen test
why check collateral circulation before an arterial stick
which artery is used for a blood gas
cards.x:
The radial artery at the wrist is usually the site of choice for an arterial sample. Before sticking it, you first check the collateral blood supply from the ulnar and radial arteries. That check is the Allen test.

Both arteries at the wrist are compressed while the hand is clenched, so the opened hand looks pale. Releasing one artery should show the flush of collateral circulation. If collateral flow is not present, another location must be chosen. The femoral and brachial arteries can also be used.

A good site has collateral blood flow, is superficial and easily accessible, and has surrounding tissues that are relatively non-sensitive. The sample can come from an arterial line or a direct arterial stick.

cards.t: Collecting and handling the arterial sample
q: how is an arterial blood gas sample collected
why does the sample go on ice
how old can a blood gas sample be
cards.x:
In outline, the patient sits or lies supine. You check collateral circulation, palpate to make sure the artery is correctly identified, and clean the site, making sure there are no signs of local infection.

Then collect a 3 to 5 mL sample in a pre-heparinized self-filling syringe, remove all air bubbles, place it on ice and send it to the lab. Indicate whether the patient was breathing room air, or describe any supplemental oxygen. The sample can only be used for an arterial blood gas if it is less than 3 hours old.

Afterward, hold pressure for a minimum of 2 minutes, or longer as needed until bleeding stops. A pressure dressing may be needed.

cards.t: Normal arterial oxygen pressure (why two cutoffs appear)
q: what is a normal arterial oxygen pressure
is normal oxygen pressure greater than 80 or 88
how does venous oxygen pressure compare with arterial
cards.x:
The normal arterial oxygen pressure is given two ways: greater than 88 mm Hg in one place and greater than 80 mm Hg in another. Do not treat one as the single truth; check which cutoff your course or lab uses.

Venous blood is far lower, 30 to 40 mm Hg, so the oxygen pressure of a venous sample cannot be read against the arterial cutoff. As with every value, read it against the range for its own sample. The arterial value helps show how well the lungs are oxygenating blood.

cards.t: When to order an arterial blood gas
q: when is an arterial blood gas indicated
what do we use a blood gas to assess
why get a baseline blood gas before surgery
cards.x:
An arterial blood gas answers a handful of specific questions, so the indications map onto the values.

- To assess oxygenation (the oxygen).
- To assess ventilation (the carbon dioxide).
- To evaluate acid-base status (the pH, bicarbonate and carbon dioxide).
- To monitor response to ongoing therapy, for example whether oxygen therapy is working; the oxygen pressure assesses how effective it is.
- To monitor critically ill patients.
- To establish baseline values before and after an operation.

If you can name which value answers your question, you know why the test is being ordered.

cards.t: What a blood gas cannot tell you
k: treat the patient not the labs
q: what are the limits of an arterial blood gas
what does treat the patient not the labs mean
does a blood gas show how severe the problem is
cards.x:
A blood gas indicates how well the lungs are oxygenating blood and whether the heart and circulation are failing. What it does not indicate is the degree of any abnormality. So you complete a physical assessment of the patient.

The guiding rule is to treat the patient and not the labs. After you read the numbers, ask the check-back question: do the labs fit the clinical presentation? That question keeps you from trusting a number over the patient.

cards.t: pH, acidosis and alkalosis (definitions and range)
q: what pH is acidosis
what is a normal blood pH
what range of pH is compatible with life
cards.x:
pH runs from 1 to 14, with 7 neutral. Acidity increases as pH falls below 7 and alkalinity increases as it rises above 7. Blood sits in a very narrow band: normal is 7.35 to 7.45, and only a range of 6.9 to 7.8 is compatible with life.

- Acidosis: pH less than 7.35.
- Alkalosis: pH greater than 7.45.

The four types of derangement are respiratory acidosis, respiratory alkalosis, metabolic acidosis and metabolic alkalosis, plus mixed disorders where more than one problem is present.

cards.t: Buffering systems that keep acid-base balance
q: what keeps blood pH stable
which organs regulate acid-base balance
what are the body's buffers
cards.x:
The body holds its acid-base balance within very narrow limits using buffering systems. The main players are the lungs and the kidneys. To a smaller extent the bones and the blood also act as buffers.

This fits the respiratory and metabolic split. The lungs handle the carbon dioxide. The kidney handles nonvolatile acids and bicarbonate. When one side goes wrong, the other can adjust to pull the pH back toward normal, which is what compensation means.

cards.t: The step-wise approach to reading a blood gas
k: how to read a blood gas
q: how do I interpret a blood gas
what is the first step in reading acid-base
how do I tell respiratory from metabolic
cards.x:
Work through any acid-base problem in the same order.

- Step 1: look at the pH. Low pH is acidosis; high pH is alkalosis.
- Step 2: find which lab values are outside normal, starting with the carbon dioxide. A primary problem with the carbon dioxide and the lungs is respiratory. A primary problem with nonvolatile acids, bicarbonate and the kidney is metabolic.
- Step 3: ask whether the labs fit the clinical presentation of the patient.

Understanding lab values and how they vary from normal is critical to diagnosis, and a fixed routine keeps you from jumping to a conclusion from one number.

cards.t: Normal arterial blood gas reference values
q: what are the normal blood gas values
what is the normal bicarbonate
what is the normal oxygen saturation
cards.x:
The reference values to know for an arterial sample:

- pH 7.35 to 7.45
- Carbon dioxide pressure 35 to 45 mm Hg
- Oxygen saturation greater than 94%
- Bicarbonate 22 to 26 mEq/L
- Carboxyhemoglobin less than 2%
- Base excess or deficit plus or minus 2 mEq/L
- Anion gap 9 to 15 (varies with the source)

The electrolytes are potassium 3.6 to 5.2 mEq/L, sodium 135 to 148 mEq/L, chloride 98 to 106 mEq/L and calcium 8.5 to 10.2 mg/dL.

The arterial oxygen pressure is not listed above because its cutoff is given two ways, greater than 88 mm Hg in some places and greater than 80 mm Hg in others, so check which range you are being held to.

cards.t: What raises or lowers the carbon dioxide
q: what causes a high carbon dioxide on a blood gas
what causes a low carbon dioxide
why does hyperventilation lower carbon dioxide
cards.x:
Carbon dioxide follows how much you breathe.

Elevated carbon dioxide is carbon dioxide retention secondary to hypoventilation, breathing too little. Causes include obstructive lung disease (emphysema, asthma, chronic bronchitis), impaired function of the respiratory center (anesthesia; drugs such as narcotics and barbiturates; head trauma), and decreased respiratory function.

Low carbon dioxide means hyperventilation, breathing too much, which blows carbon dioxide off. Causes include hypoxia, pulmonary emboli, anxiety, pain and pregnancy.

Anxiety is one to remember: hyperventilating from anxiety drives the carbon dioxide down.

cards.t: What raises or lowers the oxygen pressure
q: what causes a low oxygen pressure on a blood gas
what raises the oxygen pressure
what lowers oxygenation
cards.x:
The oxygen pressure measures dissolved oxygen, is directly influenced by the fraction of inspired oxygen, and assesses the ability to oxygenate.

Low causes: anemia; decreased atmospheric oxygen; cardiac dysfunction (cardiac decompensation); intracardiac shunts; chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and other obstructive or restrictive lung disease; pulmonary edema; pulmonary embolism; hypoventilation secondary to neuromuscular disease; and an insufficient fraction of inspired oxygen.

Elevated causes: polycythemia, an increased fraction of inspired oxygen, and hyperventilation.

Notice that the low list mixes lung problems, heart problems and simply not having enough oxygen in the air breathed.

cards.t: Compensation: respiratory vs metabolic (direction and speed)
q: how does the body compensate for acid-base disorders
which compensation is faster
what does the kidney do in respiratory acidosis
cards.x:
Compensation means the other side of the system adjusts in response to the primary problem. The two sides work at different speeds.

- Respiratory problems (carbon dioxide and the lungs) are compensated by the kidney adjusting bicarbonate reabsorption, over days. In respiratory acidosis bicarbonate increases; in respiratory alkalosis it decreases.
- Metabolic problems (nonvolatile acids, bicarbonate and the kidney) are compensated by adjusting the ventilatory rate and the carbon dioxide, over minutes to hours. In metabolic acidosis the carbon dioxide decreases (faster breathing); in metabolic alkalosis it increases.

So breathing responds quickly, while the kidney is the slow one.

cards.t: How to read compensation on a blood gas
q: how do I tell the primary problem from compensation
what does chronic respiratory acidosis look like on a gas
what does metabolic alkalosis with compensation look like
cards.x:
The pH tells you which way the primary disorder points. The value that explains that pH is the primary problem, and the other value, moving in the same direction as the primary value, is compensation.

Two examples. Long-standing lung disease with a high carbon dioxide, a low pH and a risen bicarbonate is chronic respiratory acidosis with metabolic compensation: the pH is low and the high carbon dioxide explains it, while the raised bicarbonate is the kidney pushing back.

Prolonged vomiting with a high pH, a high bicarbonate and a raised carbon dioxide is metabolic alkalosis with respiratory compensation: the high bicarbonate explains the high pH, and the raised carbon dioxide is the lungs holding back breathing to compensate.

cards.t: Quick pattern: do the arrows point the same way or opposite?
q: how can I tell respiratory from metabolic from the direction of the values
do pH and carbon dioxide move together
what happens to pH and bicarbonate in metabolic acidosis
cards.x:
A shortcut for sorting respiratory from metabolic is to check whether the values move together.

- In the metabolic disorders every arrow points the same way. In acidosis the pH, bicarbonate and carbon dioxide are all down; in alkalosis they are all up.
- In the respiratory disorders the pH and the carbon dioxide move in opposite directions: carbon dioxide up with pH down, or carbon dioxide down with pH up.

The metabolic pattern makes sense because the lungs compensate by moving the carbon dioxide the same way as the pH. Use it as a quick check, then confirm with the step-wise read.

cards.t: The four primary acid-base disorders at a glance
q: what are the four acid-base disorders
how do I tell the four disorders apart
which value is primary in each acid-base disorder
cards.x:
Each primary condition is defined by one value moving with the pH.

- Respiratory acidosis: carbon dioxide up with a low pH.
- Respiratory alkalosis: carbon dioxide down with a high pH.
- Metabolic acidosis: bicarbonate down with a low pH.
- Metabolic alkalosis: bicarbonate up with a high pH.

In the two metabolic conditions the carbon dioxide starts out normal, and compensation then lowers it in acidosis and raises it in alkalosis. In the two respiratory conditions bicarbonate starts out normal and only rises or falls later as the kidney compensates.

cards.t: Respiratory acidosis: acute vs chronic
q: what is the difference between acute and chronic respiratory acidosis
what happens to bicarbonate in chronic respiratory acidosis
what causes acute respiratory acidosis
cards.x:
Respiratory acidosis means the carbon dioxide is high and the pH is low. Acute and chronic look different in the bicarbonate.

- Acute: pH below 7.35, carbon dioxide high, bicarbonate normal. A cause is respiratory depression from drugs such as opioids, barbiturates and anesthetics.
- Chronic: the pH tries to normalize, the carbon dioxide is high, and bicarbonate rises (metabolic compensation). The cause is long-standing lung or chest wall disease.

A normal bicarbonate fits an acute problem; a risen one points to a long-standing problem.

cards.t: Causes of respiratory acidosis
q: what causes respiratory acidosis
which lung diseases cause respiratory acidosis
can heart failure cause respiratory acidosis
cards.x:
Respiratory acidosis comes from anything that stops the lungs from clearing carbon dioxide. The causes group into four themes.

- Chest wall dysfunction: thoracic cage deformities and kyphoscoliosis.
- Airway obstruction: extrathoracic tumors, asthma, bronchitis and emphysema.
- Circulatory disorders: congestive heart failure and shock.
- Acute causes: respiratory depression from drugs (opioids, barbiturates, anesthetics).

In each case, too little carbon dioxide is leaving the body, so it builds up and the blood becomes more acidic.

cards.t: Respiratory alkalosis: findings and causes
q: what causes respiratory alkalosis
what do the values look like in respiratory alkalosis
why do salicylates and sepsis cause a mixed picture
cards.x:
Respiratory alkalosis means the carbon dioxide is low and the pH is above 7.45, with a normal bicarbonate. It comes from depletion of carbon dioxide, most commonly from hyperventilation.

Causes to know:
- Stimulation of the brainstem respiratory center: emotional states (excitement, anxiety), fever and pregnancy.
- Salicylates and sepsis, both of which may cause a mixed respiratory alkalosis and metabolic acidosis.
- Cardiac disease: mild congestive heart failure leads to pulmonary edema (fast breathing).
- Mechanical over-ventilation, when a machine breathes too much for the patient.

cards.t: Metabolic acidosis: findings and causes
q: what causes metabolic acidosis
what are the lab findings in metabolic acidosis
what is the difference between acid gain and base loss
cards.x:
Metabolic acidosis means a pH below 7.35 with decreased bicarbonate. The carbon dioxide is initially normal, and compensation (faster breathing) then lowers it.

There are two ways to get there.
- Acid gain: renal failure, diabetic ketoacidosis, lactic acidosis and anaerobic metabolism.
- Loss of base: diarrhea and renal tubular acidosis.

Diabetic ketoacidosis is the one to remember. Either the body adds acid (ketoacids, lactic acid) or it loses the base that normally neutralizes acid, and in both cases bicarbonate falls and the pH drops.

cards.t: Metabolic alkalosis: findings and causes
q: what causes metabolic alkalosis
why does vomiting cause alkalosis
what are the lab findings in metabolic alkalosis
cards.x:
Metabolic alkalosis means a pH above 7.45 with increased bicarbonate. The carbon dioxide is initially normal, and compensation then raises it.

The causes are the mirror image of metabolic acidosis.
- Base gain: excessive bicarbonate administration.
- Acid loss: vomiting, and loss of gastric acids through nasogastric tube suction.
- Potassium depletion and chloride depletion.

Vomiting and suction remove gastric acid, which leaves the blood relatively too basic.

cards.t: Mixed acid-base disorders
k: mixed respiratory alkalosis and metabolic acidosis
q: what is a mixed acid-base disorder
which conditions cause mixed disorders
how can heart failure cause both respiratory and metabolic changes
cards.x:
A mixed disorder is more than one acid-base problem at the same time, instead of one primary problem with compensation.

Salicylates and sepsis may both cause a mixed respiratory alkalosis and metabolic acidosis.

Congestive heart failure shows how the picture can change over time. Mild failure leads to pulmonary edema and fast breathing, which pushes toward respiratory alkalosis. Severe failure results in hypoperfusion, then lactic acidosis, then metabolic acidosis.

cards.t: Acid-base disorders and potassium shifts
q: how does pH change potassium
why does acidosis cause hyperkalemia
what happens to potassium in alkalosis
cards.x:
Changes in pH cause changes in serum potassium, because potassium moves between the cells and the fluid outside them.

- In acidosis, potassium shifts into the extracellular space, so the blood level rises: hyperkalemia.
- In alkalosis, potassium shifts into the intracellular space, so the blood level falls: hypokalemia.

So the pH and the potassium move in opposite directions, and an abnormal potassium can follow from the pH change.

cards.t: The anion gap: what it is and the formula
q: what is the anion gap
what is the formula for the anion gap
does the anion gap include potassium
cards.x:
The anion gap is the concentration of anions other than chloride and bicarbonate. Serum albumin accounts for most of the normal anion gap. Lactate, ketones, phosphate, sulfate and other organic anions also contribute.

The formula is: anion gap = sodium minus (chloride plus bicarbonate). The normal anion gap is 9 to 15, though as with any normal it varies with the source, so a range is given when a gap must be interpreted.

One trap: potassium is not in the formula.

cards.t: How to calculate the anion gap (worked example)
q: how do I calculate the anion gap
what are common anion gap mistakes
can you show a worked anion gap example
cards.x:
Add the chloride and the bicarbonate first, then subtract that total from the sodium.

Worked example, all in mEq/L: sodium 141, chloride 103, bicarbonate 25. Chloride plus bicarbonate is 128. Then 141 minus 128 is a gap of 13, which is inside the normal range of 9 to 15.

The usual slips are to forget the bicarbonate (141 minus 103 gives 38), to add the bicarbonate instead of subtracting it, or to bring in the potassium. Remember the bicarbonate goes in with the chloride, inside the brackets, and the potassium stays out.

cards.t: Elevated anion gap and what it means
q: what causes an elevated anion gap
why is the anion gap high in diabetic ketoacidosis
what are unmeasured anions
cards.x:
An elevated anion gap means there are extra anions that the formula does not measure. Two things can produce it.

- An increase in unmeasured anions: for example anionic proteins (albumin), ketoacids, phosphate and lactate.
- A decrease in unmeasured cations: for example calcium, magnesium, potassium and gamma-globulins.

In diabetic ketoacidosis or lactic acidosis, the elevated gap reflects the extra unmeasured anions, the ketoacids and the lactate. Those anions are not counted in the formula, so they show up as a wider gap.

cards.t: Decreased anion gap and what it means
q: what causes a low anion gap
why does low albumin change the anion gap
what does lithium do to the anion gap
cards.x:
A decreased anion gap points to a short list of causes.

- An increase in unmeasured cations: for example lithium.
- Hypoalbuminemia, meaning low albumin. The gap must be corrected if albumin levels are abnormal.
- Severe hyperlipidemia, which affects the estimates of sodium and chloride.

So a low gap sends you to the albumin, to lithium, or to a lipid problem with the sodium and chloride measurements. A low albumin hides part of the gap, which is why the correction is needed.

cards.t: Correcting the anion gap for albumin
q: how do I correct the anion gap for albumin
why does low albumin hide an elevated anion gap
how much do I add for each drop in albumin
cards.x:
A low albumin hides part of the gap, so the measured gap looks smaller than it really is and you correct it upward.

The rule: add 2.5 mmol/L to the gap for each 1 g/dL of serum albumin below 4.5 g/dL. The correction moves the gap up.

For example, an albumin 1 g/dL below 4.5 means adding 2.5 to the calculated gap, and one 2 g/dL below means adding 5. Use the corrected number when deciding whether the gap is truly elevated.

cards.t: Pulmonary function testing equipment: what each device measures
q: what equipment is used for pulmonary function tests
what does a spirometer measure
what does each pulmonary function testing device measure
cards.x:
Pulmonary function testing uses a set of devices to measure lung volume, airflow, airway resistance, gas exchange, oxygenation and ventilation.

- Spirometer (handheld or desktop): airflow and some lung volumes.
- Whole-body plethysmograph: total lung capacity, functional residual capacity, residual volume and airway resistance.
- Peak flow meter: peak expiratory flow, at the bedside or at home.
- Blood gas analyzer: gas exchange and oxygenation, from a blood sample.
- Pulse oximeter: oxygenation, from a small fingertip clip.
- Calibration syringe: a calibration tool.

Results are only as good as the setup. Accurate testing depends on properly calibrated equipment, clean components and correct patient technique.

cards.t: Whole-body plethysmography (the glass booth)
q: what is whole-body plethysmography
what does a body plethysmograph measure
what is the glass booth used for in lung testing
cards.x:
Whole-body plethysmography is the lung test where the patient sits inside a glass booth and breathes through a mouthpiece. It measures four things:

- Total lung capacity: the maximum amount of air the lungs can hold.
- Functional residual capacity: the air left in the lungs after a normal, passive breath out.
- Residual volume: the air remaining after breathing out as much as possible.
- Airway resistance: how hard it is for air to flow through the bronchial tubes.

Total lung capacity is the number that confirms restriction, and lung volumes are the standard test used to look for restrictive lung disease.

cards.t: Peak flow meter
q: what does a peak flow meter measure
what is a peak flow meter used for
why do asthma patients use a peak flow meter
cards.x:
A peak flow meter measures peak expiratory flow: the maximum airflow a person can blow out in a single breath. That number correlates with the forced expiratory volume in one second, the amount of air blown out in the first second of a forced breath out.

It is used at the bedside or at home, for example to follow asthma. It is one of the specialized pulmonary function tests, not one of the three standard ones (spirometry, lung volumes and the diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide).

cards.t: Standard versus specialized pulmonary function tests
q: what are the standard pulmonary function tests
what are the specialized pulmonary function tests
which pulmonary function test points to obstruction versus restriction
cards.x:
Three tests are the standard ones, and each one points to a different kind of lung disease:

- Spirometry, including the flow-volume loop: obstructive lung disease.
- Lung volumes: restrictive lung disease.
- Diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide, which measures the integrity of the alveolar-capillary membrane (the barrier gas crosses between air sacs and blood): pulmonary vascular disease.

The specialized tests are:

- Arterial blood gas.
- Exercise oximetry: oxygenation at rest and with modest activity; quick and cheap.
- Six-minute walk test: walking as far as possible in 6 minutes, to monitor response to treatment as well as prognosis.
- Peak flow: the maximum expiratory airflow delivered in a single breath, as in asthma.
- Maximal inspiratory and expiratory pressures: diaphragmatic strength and the neurologic side of breathing.

cards.t: The six-minute walk test
q: what is the six-minute walk test
what does the six-minute walk test measure
why do patients do a six-minute walk
cards.x:
The six-minute walk test is a specialized pulmonary function test. The patient walks as far as possible in 6 minutes. It is used to monitor response to treatment as well as prognosis.

It is not one of the three standard tests (spirometry, lung volumes and the diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide).

cards.t: The four lung volumes
q: what are the four lung volumes
what is tidal volume
what is residual volume
what is the difference between a lung volume and a lung capacity
cards.x:
A lung volume is one single compartment of the air in the lungs. There are four.

- Tidal volume: the air moved in and out with each normal restful breath, about 500 mL (it varies with age, sex and size).
- Inspiratory reserve volume: the extra air breathed in on top of a tidal breath, 3000 to 3300 mL.
- Expiratory reserve volume: the extra air breathed out after a normal breath out.
- Residual volume: the air still in the lungs after breathing out as much as possible. It can never be breathed out. 1200 mL.

A capacity is different: it is a sum of volumes.

cards.t: The four lung capacities
q: what are the four lung capacities
what is functional residual capacity
what is vital capacity
how is total lung capacity calculated
cards.x:
A lung capacity is a sum of two or more lung volumes. There are four.

- Inspiratory capacity: tidal volume plus inspiratory reserve volume, the breath that can be drawn in from the end of a quiet breath out.
- Functional residual capacity: expiratory reserve volume plus residual volume. It is the air left in the lungs at the end of a quiet breath out, with all the respiratory muscles fully relaxed (2200 to 2400 mL).
- Vital capacity: tidal plus inspiratory reserve plus expiratory reserve volume. It is everything except the residual volume, from the deepest breath in to the fullest breath out (4500 to 5000 mL).
- Total lung capacity: all four volumes added together, the maximum volume the lungs can hold (5700 to 6200 mL).

cards.t: Reading the lung volume tracing
q: how do I read the lung volumes and capacities tracing
where is residual volume on the spirometry tracing
how do I find functional residual capacity on the diagram
cards.x:
The tracing records quiet (tidal) breaths, then one deepest breath in, then one fullest breath out. Read it like this:

- The small rise and fall of each quiet breath is the tidal volume.
- From the top of a quiet breath up to the peak of the deepest breath is the inspiratory reserve volume.
- From the end of a quiet breath out down to the lowest point of the fullest breath out is the expiratory reserve volume.
- Below that lowest point is the residual volume. The tracing itself never goes below the expiratory reserve volume, because the residual volume cannot be breathed out.
- The expiratory reserve volume plus the residual volume, from the end of a quiet breath out to the bottom, is the functional residual capacity.

This is a diagram worth knowing well enough to redraw from memory.

cards.t: How spirometry is done
q: how is spirometry performed
how long does the patient blow out in spirometry
how many times is spirometry repeated
cards.x:
Spirometry measures air flow and some lung volumes. The patient places the mouth around the mouthpiece, breathes in as deeply as possible, then blows out forcefully, as fast as possible, and keeps going for at least 6 seconds.

The effort is repeated 3 times, and the highest air volumes and flows are the ones recorded. The result comes out as two graphs, a volume-time curve and a flow-volume loop, and the numbers read from them are the forced values.

cards.t: The forced spirometry values: forced vital capacity, FEV1, peak flow and more
k: forced expiratory volume in one second
q: what is FEV1
what is forced vital capacity
what are the values measured on spirometry
which spirometry values matter most
cards.x:
Every forced value comes from a hard, fast breath out after a maximal breath in.

- Forced vital capacity (FVC): the total volume that can be blown out forcefully and rapidly, typically reached in about 6 seconds.
- Forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1): the amount blown out in the first second.
- FEV1/FVC ratio: a calculated value, the percentage of the forced vital capacity exhaled in the first second.
- Peak expiratory flow rate: the maximum velocity during the forced breath out, the top of the flow-volume loop.
- Forced expiratory volume in 6 seconds: the volume blown out by 6 seconds.
- Forced expiratory flow 25% to 75%: the average flow over the middle half of the forced vital capacity.

The three most important are the forced vital capacity, the forced expiratory volume in one second and the ratio of the two.

cards.t: The normal volume-time curve
q: what does the normal volume-time curve look like
how do you read FEV1 and FVC on the volume-time curve
what is the plateau on a spirometry curve
cards.x:
The volume-time curve plots the volume blown out against time. In a normal test it rises steeply and then levels off in a plateau. Three readings come off it:

- The volume at 1 second is the forced expiratory volume in one second.
- The plateau, reached by about 6 seconds, is the forced vital capacity.
- The steepest part of the slope is the peak expiratory flow rate.

Normally more than 80% of the forced vital capacity is blown out in the first second, so the first second of a normal curve is steep.

cards.t: The normal flow-volume loop
q: what is a flow-volume loop
what does a normal flow-volume loop look like
where is peak expiratory flow on the loop
cards.x:
The flow-volume loop is the graph of airflow against lung volume during a forced breath in and a forced breath out in spirometry. The expiratory limb sits above the horizontal axis and the inspiratory limb below it.

The top of the expiratory limb is the peak expiratory flow. From that peak the normal expiratory limb falls in a straight line down to the volume axis. The vital capacity spans the loop.

Know the normal loop and the abnormal ones follow from it.

cards.t: Normal ranges for pulmonary function results
q: what are the normal values for pulmonary function tests
what is a normal FEV1
what is a normal total lung capacity
what ratio means obstruction
cards.x:
Results are compared with a predicted (reference) value, and normal is given as a percent of that predicted value:

- Forced expiratory volume in one second and forced vital capacity: 80% to 100%.
- The ratio of the two: within 5% of predicted.
- Total lung capacity: 80% to 120%.
- Functional residual capacity and residual volume: 75% to 120%.
- Diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide: more than 60%.

Separately, the ratio is the percentage of the forced vital capacity blown out in the first second: normal is more than 80%, and below 70% indicates obstruction.

cards.t: Why order pulmonary function tests (diagnosing a symptom)
q: why do we order pulmonary function tests
what is the most common reason for pulmonary function tests
do pulmonary function tests give a specific diagnosis
cards.x:
The most common reason to order pulmonary function tests is to help diagnose a patient with a lung symptom, such as chronic shortness of breath, cough, or unexplained hypercapnia (too much carbon dioxide in the blood) or hypoxemia (too little oxygen in the blood). Smokers and people with occupational exposures are examples.

The tests do not give a specific diagnosis. They show what kind of functional problem (pathophysiological derangement) the underlying disease is causing, and they help rule parts of the differential (the list of possible diagnoses) out.

cards.t: Pulmonary function tests for prognosis, surgical risk and screening
q: what are the other reasons to order pulmonary function tests
why test lung function before lung surgery
why do patients on amiodarone get pulmonary function tests
cards.x:
Besides diagnosing a symptom, pulmonary function tests are ordered for three other reasons.

- Prognosis: they can help determine the outlook in a patient with known disease.
- Surgical risk: they can estimate the risk in patients facing lung resection or with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.
- Screening: they can catch early, asymptomatic complications from non-pulmonary diseases such as autoimmune diseases, or from medication. One example is long-term amiodarone, which can cause significant pulmonary toxicity.

cards.t: The three categories: obstructive, restrictive and pulmonary vascular
q: how do pulmonary function tests classify lung disease
what is gas transfer impairment
can a lung disease be both obstructive and restrictive
cards.x:
Pulmonary function tests sort diffuse lung disease into three categories: obstructive, restrictive and pulmonary vascular (also called gas transfer impairment).

The third group has normal breathing mechanics. The problem is oxygen and carbon dioxide moving across the alveolar-capillary membrane, or the pulmonary blood flow (the delivery of hemoglobin to the membrane). Examples are pulmonary hypertension, chronic thromboembolic disease, early emphysema and early interstitial lung disease. Because the mechanics are normal, its curves and loops look normal, and the diffusing capacity is what finds it.

The categories are not mutually exclusive. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease can have both obstructive and vascular components, and sarcoidosis can be restrictive, obstructive and vascular.

cards.t: Obstructive lung disease: air gets in but can't get out
q: what is obstructive lung disease
what conditions cause an obstructive pattern
what is bronchiectasis
cards.x:
Obstructive lung disease means decreased airflow. Airway resistance is increased, so air gets in but has trouble getting out.

Examples are chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (chronic bronchitis and emphysema), asthma, asthmatic or chronic obstructive bronchitis, cystic fibrosis and bronchiectasis. Bronchiectasis is permanent dilation of the airways, resulting in chronic inflammation, recurrent infections and increased airway resistance.

On spirometry the telltale sign is a low ratio of the forced expiratory volume in one second to the forced vital capacity, below 70%.

cards.t: Restrictive lung disease: trouble getting air in
q: what is restrictive lung disease
what conditions cause a restrictive pattern
why do neuromuscular diseases cause restriction
cards.x:
Restrictive lung disease means a decrease in volume. The cause is either poor compliance of the respiratory system, so the lungs need more effort to expand than normal, or neuromuscular impairment. Either way the breaths are shallow: the trouble is getting air in.

Examples:
- Interstitial lung diseases (pulmonary fibrosis, sarcoidosis).
- Chest wall problems (obesity, kyphosis, scoliosis).
- Neuromuscular diseases (amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, muscular dystrophy). These impair lung function through weakness of the respiratory muscles rather than poor compliance.

Other named causes are beryllium disease, congestive heart failure, idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, interstitial pneumonitis and thoracic deformities.

cards.t: The FEV1/FVC ratio: obstruction versus restriction
q: why does the FEV1/FVC ratio fall in obstruction
what happens to the ratio in restrictive lung disease
how do FEV1 and FVC differ in obstruction and restriction
cards.x:
The ratio is the forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) divided by the forced vital capacity (FVC): the percentage of the FVC exhaled in the first second. The marker is 70%.

In obstruction it takes longer to push the air out, so FEV1 drops proportionally more than FVC and the ratio falls below 70%.

In restriction the FVC itself is the value that is decreased, so the ratio stays normal or rises, 70% or more.

- Obstructive: FEV1 normal (very mild) or decreased (moderate or severe); FVC normal (mild or moderate) or decreased (severe); ratio decreased, below 70%.
- Restrictive: FEV1 normal or decreased; FVC decreased; ratio normal or increased.

cards.t: Volume-time curve patterns: normal, obstructive and restrictive
q: what does an obstructive volume-time curve look like
how does the restrictive volume-time curve differ from normal
what does the spirometry curve look like in restriction
cards.x:
Compare the three shapes.

- Normal: a steep rise, with more than 80% of the forced vital capacity out in the first second, then a plateau.
- Obstruction: a slow rise with no steep first second, and a long, late plateau. In mild obstruction the plateau is late but the forced vital capacity is preserved; in severe obstruction there is no plateau and the forced vital capacity is reduced. The obstructive pattern is determined by the ratio.
- Restriction: the normal shape, a steep rise and a normal plateau, but at a lower volume because the forced vital capacity is reduced. The air comes out easily; there is simply less of it.

In one example, the normal tracing blew out 80% of the forced vital capacity in the first second and the obstructed one only 47%.

cards.t: Flow-volume loop patterns: the scoop and the witch's hat
q: what does an obstructive flow-volume loop look like
what is coving
what does a restrictive flow-volume loop look like
cards.x:
Think of three shapes.

- Normal: a quick rise to a sharp peak, then an expiratory limb that falls in a straight line.
- Obstruction, the "scoop in the loop": after the peak the expiratory limb is scooped inward (concave). That deformity is called coving. In mild obstruction the peak expiratory flow is mildly reduced, with coving. In severe obstruction the peak is severely reduced and the limb collapses into a long flat tail, still with coving.
- Restriction, the witch's hat: narrow and tall with a sharp point, and everything is smaller because less volume moves. Peak expiratory flow is normal or mildly reduced, and there is no coving.

Gas transfer impairment keeps normal breathing mechanics, so its loops look normal.

cards.t: Obstruction versus restriction on the chest film
q: what does a chest film look like in obstructive lung disease
how do I tell obstruction from restriction in a breathless patient
what does a chest film look like in restrictive lung disease
cards.x:
Two patients with the same complaint, breathlessness on exertion, can have opposite problems.

A 62-year-old former smoker who also wheezes, with a film showing hyperinflated lungs and flat diaphragms, fits obstruction.

A 66-year-old nonsmoker with a dry cough and "Velcro" crackles, whose film shows small-volume lungs with reticular opacities (a net-like pattern), fits restriction, and a low total lung capacity confirms it.

So the film can hint at the pattern: hyperinflated lungs fit obstruction, and small-volume lungs with reticular opacities fit restriction.

cards.t: Obstructive versus restrictive: how to tell them apart
q: what is the difference between obstructive and restrictive lung disease
how do obstruction and restriction look different on spirometry
how do the flow-volume loops differ in obstruction and restriction
cards.x:
Obstruction is trouble getting air out; restriction is trouble getting air in (a decrease in volume).

- Ratio of the forced expiratory volume in one second to the forced vital capacity: decreased, below 70%, in obstruction; normal or increased, 70% or more, in restriction.
- Forced vital capacity: normal or decreased in obstruction (decreased when severe); decreased in restriction.
- Volume-time curve: obstruction rises slowly to a late plateau; restriction has the normal shape at a lower volume.
- Flow-volume loop: obstruction is scooped after the peak (coving); restriction is narrow and tall, like a witch's hat, with no coving.
- Total lung capacity: a low value points to restriction.

cards.t: Reading a pulmonary function report step by step
q: how do I interpret a pulmonary function test report
what do I look at first on spirometry
low ratio and low FVC means what
cards.x:
A report is a page of numbers, so read it in a fixed order.

1. Look at the ratio (forced expiratory volume in one second over forced vital capacity) first.
2. If the ratio is low, look at the forced vital capacity. A low forced vital capacity means obstruction or a mixed pattern (severe obstruction can reduce the forced vital capacity too). A normal forced vital capacity means obstruction.
3. If the ratio is normal or high, look at the forced vital capacity. A low value means possible restriction. A normal or high value means normal lung mechanics.

Lung volumes (the total lung capacity) then confirm restriction, since they are the standard test for it.

cards.t: Total lung capacity: confirming restriction and spotting a mixed defect
q: what does a low total lung capacity mean
what is a mixed defect on pulmonary function tests
how do I tell obstruction from a mixed defect
cards.x:
Two numbers tell you the main pattern.

- A low ratio means obstruction.
- A low total lung capacity means restriction.
- Both low together is obstruction and restriction at once, called a mixed defect.

So a low total lung capacity is restriction, and when the ratio is normal there is no obstruction alongside it.

Total lung capacity also settles the question left by spirometry. A low ratio with a low forced vital capacity could be obstruction or a mixed defect. If the total lung capacity is not low (for example 7.1 L, 120%, with a residual volume of 216%), the answer is obstruction, not a mixed defect.

cards.t: Grading the severity of obstruction
q: how do the numbers change as obstruction gets worse
what FEV1 is severe obstruction
what peak flow goes with severe obstruction
cards.x:
As obstruction worsens, the forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1), the ratio and the peak flow all fall. Example values:

- Normal: FEV1 about 4.0 to 6.0 L, ratio 80 to 90, peak flow 550 to 650 L/min in men or 400 to 500 in women.
- Mild: FEV1 3.0 L, ratio 70, peak flow 300 to 400.
- Moderate: FEV1 1.6 L, ratio 50, peak flow 200 to 300.
- Severe: FEV1 0.6 L, ratio 40, peak flow 100.

These are worked examples. The pattern to remember is that all three numbers drop together.

cards.t: What restrictive spirometry numbers look like
q: what do the numbers look like in restriction
why is the ratio normal or high in restriction
what does a high FEV1/FVC ratio with a low FVC mean
cards.x:
A restrictive report shows a low forced vital capacity with a normal or high ratio. In one example, the forced vital capacity was 0.96 L against 2.75 L predicted (35% of predicted). The forced expiratory volume in one second was 0.94 against 1.90 (49%). The ratio was 98% (against a predicted 69%), and the peak expiratory flow was 55% of predicted.

The ratio is high because the forced vital capacity fell even more than the forced expiratory volume in one second did (35% against 49% of predicted). The air comes out easily; there is just far less of it. A normal or high ratio with a low forced vital capacity means possible restriction, which the total lung capacity then confirms.

cards.t: Worked example: obstruction in a 56-year-old smoker
q: what does a pulmonary function report for obstruction look like
how do I tell obstruction from a mixed defect in a smoker
does a low FVC with a low ratio mean mixed disease
cards.x:
A 56-year-old smoker has had a productive cough and dyspnea (shortness of breath) for more than 3 months. The patient is thin and comfortable, with an oxygen saturation of 95% on room air and diminished breath sounds throughout both lungs.

- The ratio is 52% against a reference of 82%: low, so the next step is the forced vital capacity.
- The forced vital capacity is 2.3 L, 61% of reference: low, which reads as obstruction or mixed.
- The total lung capacity is 7.1 L, 120%, not low (the residual volume is 216%), so this is obstruction, not a mixed defect.
- The flow-volume loop is scooped, and the diffusing capacity is 73%.
- Testing before and after the inhaled drug albuterol changes little.

Low ratio, low forced vital capacity, a total lung capacity that is not low and a scooped loop: obstruction.

cards.t: Worked example: restriction with a low diffusing capacity
q: what does a restrictive pulmonary function report look like
what does a low diffusing capacity mean in restriction
how do I confirm restriction
cards.x:
A 32-year-old animal trainer has a progressive dry cough and dyspnea (shortness of breath) for the past month, with mild respiratory discomfort. Heart rate is 104, respiratory rate 28 and oxygen saturation 88% on room air, with fine crackles throughout both lungs.

- The ratio is 94% against a reference of 84%: normal or high.
- The forced vital capacity is 1.7 L, 39%: low, so possible restriction.
- The total lung capacity of 2.5 L, 44%, confirms it.
- The diffusing capacity is low, 38% (10 against 26): gas is not crossing the alveolar-capillary membrane normally.
- The loop is narrow.

High ratio, low forced vital capacity and total lung capacity, low diffusing capacity and a narrow loop: restriction.
